rounds.proof_sketch: Kernel launch: blocks = batch_size = 128, so blockIdx.x ∈ [0, 127]. Original guard: batch_idx >= 128 → always false. Mutated guard: batch_idx >= 129 → always false. Both conditions are universally false for all launched blocks, making the mutation dead code.
rounds.survival_reason: The CUDA kernel is launched with exactly `batch_size = 128` blocks, which means `blockIdx.x` (assigned to `batch_idx`) can only take values from 0 to 127 inclusive. The original boundary check `batch_idx >= batch_size` (i.e., `batch_idx >= 128`) is a safety guard that can never trigger since no block will have index 128 or higher. The mutated condition `batch_idx >= batch_size + 1` (i.e., `batch_idx >= 129`) is equally unreachable - both evaluate to false for all valid block indices [0, 127]. Since neither condition ever evaluates to true, both versions execute identical code paths for all blocks, processing all 128 batch elements identically.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects a boundary guard that is never triggered because CUDA launch parameters guarantee block indices stay within [0, batch_size-1]. No value-level input can cause the mutated predicate to behave differently from the original since both are always false for valid block indices.
rounds.recommendations: When writing boundary guards in CUDA kernels, consider that guards protecting against blockIdx exceeding the grid size are already enforced by CUDA's launch semantics. Such guards are defensive programming but represent dead code under normal operation. Mutation testing of such guards will always produce equivalent mutants unless the guard affects values within the valid index range.
